To bridge these two aspects, we present RIGOR: a large-scale reconstruction pipeline for gravity-aligned omnidirectional videos that retains a frozen feed-forward perspective backbone and exploits each panorama as a four-view virtual rig. The rig structure is used to detect and repair locally inconsistent predictions, to retrieve loop closures through cyclic four-view consensus, and to geometrically verify candidate revisits before global optimization. Verified constraints drive a Sim(3) pose graph that corrects accumulated rotation, translation, and scale drift along the sequence. We demonstrate that the proposed consistency mechanisms improve both trajectory accuracy and reconstructed geometry over a feed-forward baseline on challenging construction-site sequences. The code is made available under this link: https://github.com/TangentH/RIGOR.
authors: Tingjun Huang, Dmitry Rudshin, Mathieu Meyer, Pietro Bonazzi, Marc Pollefeys, Emilia Szymanska
entries.title: RIGOR: Rig-Informed Geometry for Omnidirectional Reconstruction

entries.abstract: Semantic watermarks for diffusion models embed ownership information into the generative process while preserving perceptual quality, but Gaussian-Shading extraction conventionally requires multi-step diffusion inversion to recover the initial noise. Recent one-step methods show that this cost can be reduced substantially. We study this problem through extended flow matching and conditional regression. The key observation is that, near the high-SNR image endpoint, recovering a useful noise statistic given by the first-step output of the extended flow matching in the high-SNR regime is much simpler than reconstructing the full inverse trajectory, and Gaussian Shading only requires the recovered latent to remain in the correct watermark decision region. Based on this observation, we propose a lightweight, prompt-free extractor that decomposes endpoint recovery into an image-like anchor and a noise-oriented residual, which increases the capability of the model to utilize GPU parallel computation. The resulting method avoids iterative inversion and repeated evaluation of a diffusion-scale U-Net, providing an efficient one-step extraction pipeline with a concise theoretical interpretation. The computational cost of extracting noise is lower than that of both OSI and FARI. The github repo is there: https://github.com/TheLovesOfLadyPurple/RAIN-lightweight-NN-for-one-step-semantic-watermark-extraction
authors: Zilai Li
entries.title: RAIN: Region-Aware Inversion Network for Semantic Watermark Extraction

entries.abstract: Bone overlap can obscure abnormalities in chest radiographs, while scarce paired training data limit supervised bone suppression. We address this challenge with a digitally reconstructed radiograph (DRR) framework that converts chest computed tomography (CT) into paired supervision for component suppression. A novel bone segmentation algorithm enables CT decomposition into bone, non-lung soft-tissue, and lung components, which are projected separately. Their weighted combination yields synthetic radiographs with pixel-registered component images that sum exactly to the full DRR. Models trained on these data suppress bone or lung components by predicting the target component and recovering the remainder by subtraction, transferring to real radiographs without real paired training data. As an extension, their outputs on real radiographs provide target domains for unpaired, component-wise DRR translation, reducing the appearance gap while retaining anatomical details. Across multiple public datasets, downstream detection experiments demonstrate the utility of bone suppression, with gains concentrated on abnormalities with substantial bone overlap. Compared with open-source DRR engines applied to the same CTs, our unmodified DRRs achieve comparable realism and preservation of label-relevant anatomy, while translated DRRs achieve the best Fr\'echet inception distance (FID), lung-field sharpness, and agreement with source-CT anatomy among the evaluated methods. Models and inference code: https://huggingface.co/qureaiorg/bone-suppression ; Translated projections: https://huggingface.co/datasets/qureaiorg/ct2xr-projections.
authors: Mrunmay Angaitkar, Piyush Kumar, Aarjav Satia, Pranav Rao, Ashish Mittal, Manoj Tadepalli, Preetham Putha
entries.title: Anatomy-Decomposed Chest Computed Tomography (CT) Projections as Scalable Supervision for Bone Suppression in Chest Radiographs

entries.abstract:
Raw 3D point clouds are a core geometric representation. Establishing their ownership is challenging because point sets are irregular, unstructured, and frequently altered by resampling and geometric preprocessing. We present a blind watermarking framework that operates directly on xyz coordinates and supports both object-level shapes and scene-scale scans. At verification time, the embedded message is recovered from the observed point cloud alone, without access to the original point cloud, color, normals, or mesh connectivity. The method jointly learns watermark embedding and extraction through a feed-forward octree-based architecture, enabling efficient multi-scale geometric reasoning on large point sets. During training, a stochastic transformation layer exposes the decoder to common geometric perturbations, while progressive pose alignment improves robustness to pose changes.
  Experiments on object-level and scene-level benchmarks demonstrate reliable message recovery under common geometric processing while maintaining low geometric distortion. Qualitative comparisons further show that the learned perturbations are less visually conspicuous and less spatially structured than those of handcrafted alternatives.
authors: Rungui Zhou, Chuanzhi Zhou, Ruihuan Wang, Peng-Shuai Wang
entries.title: Geometry-Preserving Blind Watermarking for Raw 3D Point Clouds

entries.abstract: Multi-camera pedestrian detection and tracking often require camera calibration, position annotations, and target-scene training. CAT-Free removes all three requirements and uses only synchronized RGB video. From this video, CAT-Free estimates camera poses and the ground plane. With the estimated poses and ground plane, CAT-Free triangulates detections across cameras and links pedestrian positions into tracks. However, camera errors and mismatched detections produce false positions. Two geometric filters remove these false positions: one rejects unstable estimates, and the other rejects positions off the ground. Both filter thresholds are estimated from the unlabeled video. Without calibration, annotations, or target-scene training, CAT-Free achieves 89.2, 84.1, and 76.1 MODA on WildTrack, MultiviewX, and GMVD. CAT-Free is also less affected by camera errors than methods that assume known camera parameters, and it outperforms a domain adaptation method without any adaptation.
authors: Taigo Sakai, Hiroki Kouno, Naoki Kato, Kazuhiro Hotta
entries.title: CAT-Free: Calibration-, Annotation-, and Target-Training-Free Multi-View BEV Pedestrian Detection and Tracking

entries.abstract: Reliable visual question answering requires correct answers when evidence is sufficient and abstention when it is not. We introduce a benchmark of 3,000 question groups: 1,000 each from PlotQA charts, CLEVR rendered scenes, and GQA photographs. Each group keeps the question fixed across original, answer-preserving, and evidence-removing images; charts and CLEVR also include answer-changing edits. Models receive each image independently. A group succeeds only if every supported answer and every required abstention is correct. For charts and CLEVR, executable witnesses establish ambiguity under the declared task semantics: two admissible complete charts or scenes give different answers but yield the same masked observation. GQA scoring compares source labels with a permissive rule that also credits masked-image answers compatible with the full-image reference. Across 72,000 responses from six model configurations, the best complete-question success is 57.0% on charts, 43.5% on CLEVR, and 33.7% on GQA under source labels. On charts, the strongest configuration makes correct answer-or-abstain decisions on 96.2% of individual images and on all five images of 83.5% of questions. Requiring correct answers lowers success to 57.0%: in 26.5% of all chart questions, every decision is correct but at least one answer is wrong. Adding answer correctness also reverses a chart ranking based on decision accuracy. Evaluating all response obligations together reveals failures that per-image decision accuracy conceals.
authors: Sungguk Cha, Mintae Kim, Youngsub Han, Byoung-Ki Jeon, Sangyeob Lee
entries.title: When Does an Image Determine the Answer? Benchmarking Visual Answerability across Charts and Scenes

entries.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown great promise for robotic manipulation by mapping multi-modal semantics to physical actions. However, this mapping inherently struggles to align these coarse-grained semantics with fine-grained temporal execution. It leaves VLA models with limited generalization and insufficient robustness in cluttered environments. To overcome this issue, we propose ActionUNet, an efficient multi-scale fine-tuning framework that enhances pre-trained VLA models with minimal computational cost. ActionUNet first constructs a lightweight temporal U-Net within the temporal-aligned action feature space to fuse hierarchical structural priors, effectively bridging the scale gap between semantics and temporal executions. Recognizing that multi-scale modeling can disrupt microscopic temporal continuity and cause mechanical oscillations, ActionUNet then employs a conditional SIREN as a continuous action decoder. Equipped with explicit second-order smoothness constraints, this decoder guarantees temporal continuity and reduces high-frequency motion jitter. By smoothing temporal discontinuities from multi-scale fusion, this continuous formulation reduces mechanical execution failures while preserving the base VLA model's generalization and manipulation robustness. Extensive experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks, together with real-world hard evaluations, demonstrate that ActionUNet significantly improves {\pi}0.5 success rates by absolute 9.8%, 6.1%, and 11.4%, respectively, while also generalizing to the regression-based OpenVLA-OFT backbone, highlighting its effectiveness and efficiency as a fine-tuning strategy. Code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/Di-Zhu123/ActionUNet.
authors: Di Zhu, Ziheng Yan, Fang Wan
entries.title: ActionUNet: Improving Robustness of VLA Models with Efficient Multi-scale Fine-tuning

entries.abstract: World action models integrate future visual dynamics with robot action prediction, but their scalability remains limited by the need for action-annotated robot trajectories. Observation-only videos contain rich evidence about interaction dynamics, but existing approaches typically use them either to pretrain visual representations that must later be adapted for control, or to infer latent actions that are subsequently grounded to robot commands. We present NAVA-WAM, which introduces native action-prior learning by directly pretraining the action policy from observation-only videos, avoiding indirect representation-to-control transfer or a separate latent-action model. Our training consists of two stages. First, we pretrain on observation-only videos, where future-video flow-matching supervision over visual transitions is propagated through transition-structured joint attention to optimize the Action-DiT and learn action-relevant priors. Second, we use action-labeled demonstrations to post-train the Action-DiT for robot control through joint video--action flow matching, while asymmetric attention decouples the visual branch from iterative action denoising and enables efficient action-only inference. Extensive experiments show that NAVA-WAM consistently outperforms prior approaches under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, while demonstrating strong action-label efficiency and effective real-robot generalization. These results establish native action-prior learning as an effective approach to directly pretrain action policies from observation-only videos, providing a scalable path beyond action-labeled robot data.
authors: Zhaochong An, Fei Zhang, Menglin Jia, Duncan Frost, Zijian Zhou, Yikai Wang, Xudong Wang, Aditya Patel, Belinda Zeng, Tao Xiang, Serge Belongie, Amir Bar, Sen He
entries.title: Native Action-Prior Learning from Videos for World Action Models

entries.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) have shown increasing potential for clinical image interpretation. However, these models still struggle to interpret multi-phenotype lesions whose diagnosis requires the joint assessment of multiple pathological phenotypes. Existing vision-language alignment methods produce visual representations that fail to preserve anatomical hierarchies and relationships among phenotypic subclasses. This stems from their reliance on semantic supervision, which lacks geometric constraints to preserve these relationships in the visual embedding space. Moreover, the sparsity of lesion-related anatomical and phenotypic representations makes it difficult for medical VLMs to capture important diagnostic evidence. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{PureVision}, a geometry-supervised visual representation learning framework for multi-phenotype lesion interpretation in medical VLMs. It combines a geometry-supervised representation learning module, \textbf{PureEyes}, and an anatomy-guided evidence aggregation module, \textbf{PureNeurons}. PureEyes provides geometric supervision through ideal spatial distributions that encode anatomical hierarchies and phenotypic subclass relationships. PureNeurons projects visual representations into the learned latent space, using their positions to selectively aggregate lesion-specific anatomical and phenotypic evidence. Experiments on \textit{LIDC-IDRI}, \textit{CBIS-DDSM}, and \textit{3DReasonKnee} demonstrate that PureVision improves lesion grounding and phenotype characterization in visual question answering and radiology report generation. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/purevision-06C2.
authors: Hao Wang, Qiwei Zeng, Shuchang Ye, Jinghao Lin, Yuezhe Yang, Yige Peng, Jinman Kim, Lei Bi
entries.title: Geometry-Supervised Visual Representation Learning for Multi-Phenotype Lesion Interpretation in Medical VLMs

entries.abstract: Dense correspondence matching has historically been bounded by simplifying spatio-temporal priors, such as smooth motion and rigid geometry. While effective for classical tasks, these assumptions break down in image editing and reference-guided generation (IEG), where transformations can preserve visual identity while breaking physical continuity. To establish identity-preserving correspondence across such transformations, we introduce FreeMatching, a generalizable framework combining generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes. Teacher-guided iterative refinement further improves correspondence in IEG without dense correspondence annotations. Experimentally, a single FreeMatching model substantially improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG image pairs while retaining competitive performance on classical benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility as a quantitative metric for evaluating identity preservation, with scores that correlate with human judgment. The code is available at https://github.com/luping-liu/FreeMatching.
authors: Luping Liu, Bingyi Kang, Yifan Wang, Dong Xu
entries.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal Priors: A Generalizable Approach for Dense Correspondence Matching

entries.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.
authors: Senbin Xu, Zijun Zhang, Xinhua Wu, Li He, Jubo Feng, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Yan Zhang, Jixiang Luo, Rongrong Ji
entries.title: SPARE: Shared Perception and Adaptive Retrieval of Evidence for Streaming Video Understanding

entries.abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yuheng98chen/RPD-Unidoc
authors: Yuheng Chen, Yufan Chen, Zhuojun Cai, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Weijia Fan, Kunyu Peng, Jiaming Zhang, Rainer Stiefelhagen
entries.title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation

entries.abstract: Surgical teams could benefit from assistants that watch the video for requested events, such as "tell me when the clip applier appears during Calot triangle dissection", and answer questions about what has already happened. We formalise this task as request-driven event detection with exact semantics and causal alert decisions, and present SurgStreamer. It separates procedure-specific perception, which maps the 1-FPS stream to a structured state over tools, actions and phases, from procedure-agnostic reasoning, which evaluates a formal monitoring condition over this state and an event memory, either with exact rules or with a small controller that addresses entities through pointers rather than names. We evaluate this monitoring core with gold conditions. On a pre-registered, sealed test set of 12 laparoscopic cholecystectomies, SurgStreamer reached a macro event-F1 of 0.598 over full procedures. On identical 75-s windows with only the window available to every method, it scored 0.677. The tested configurations of the streaming vision-language model OneStreamer-4B, including ones fine-tuned on SurgStreamer's state or on video with an adapted vision encoder, scored at most 0.540 (Holm-adjusted p <= 0.012). At three external centres, re-training only perception raised performance on held-out procedures from 0.239 to 0.470. On a new procedure, pituitary surgery, controller weights trained on cholecystectomy matched an in-domain controller on oracle state (0.947 vs 0.938). On predicted state they missed the pre-registered non-inferiority margin (-0.024 [-0.040, -0.008]) unless the alert thresholds were re-calibrated. The results support separating perception from reasoning and point to perception under distribution shift as the main limitation.
authors: Bowen Xiang, Jon S. Heiselman
entries.title: SurgStreamer: proactive, request-driven monitoring of surgical video streams with structured state and a reusable reasoning layer

entries.abstract: As joint audio-video generation models become more capable, they can generate audio-visual scenes exhibiting three forms of complexity: multi-event composition, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. However, current evaluations largely reuse metrics from earlier simple and unidirectional tasks. They typically evaluate an audio-video clip as a whole and rely on simple predefined relations, making them unsuitable for these increasingly complex scenes. We propose an event-centric evaluation framework that disentangles audio and visual events at the event level, analyzes each event independently, cross-validates relations across modalities, and aggregates the judgments into a coarse-to-fine, three-level consistency metric. The metric assesses global narrative harmony, event-level temporal synchronization, and fine-grained attribute alignment, providing a general formulation for audio-video consistency evaluation across diverse generation settings and cross-modal relations. We instantiate the metric as AVC-Reward, a trainable audio-video reward model. To evaluate the agreement between automatic judgments and human perception across generation paradigms and relation complexities, we construct AVC-Benchmark, which is primarily built from diverse positive and negative samples generated by various types of audio-video generation models. AVC-Reward achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human judgment among automatic methods, provides interpretable rationales that localize failures, and improves the audio-video consistency of a joint generation model when used as an online reinforcement-learning signal. Project page: https://tsuki0512.github.io/AVC-Reward.github.io/
authors: Yuruo Wu, Kaihang Pan, Kai Shen, Jiacheng Li, Shuyuan Tu, Li Tuoyu, Juncheng Li, Siliang Tang
entries.title: AVC-Reward: Event-Centric Audio-Video Consistency Evaluation

entries.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon path planning grounded in the currently observed geometry. Anticipating how future observations evolve along the instructed route provides predictive guidance beyond the current field of view, motivating video-action models (VAMs) that learn representations of future visual states. However, many existing VAMs couple future visual prediction with action generation during inference, despite their distinct temporal requirements: instruction-conditioned route guidance can be reused across multiple control steps, whereas local trajectories must continuously adapt to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while zero-shot real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments.
authors: Dongzhihan Wang, Yi Du, Chen Wang, Xiuxian Li, Liang Xu
entries.title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation

entries.abstract: Image-to-Video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single portrait or photograph, enabling shared images to be repurposed for motion synthesis without the subject's authorization. We study proactive visual protection against such use: before an image is released, its owner applies a bounded perturbation that preserves the sharing workflow but disrupts downstream motion generation. Existing spectral disruption objectives globally attenuate temporal representations and therefore provide limited control over subtle or spatially localized motion. Our key idea is that generated dynamics depend not only on temporal feature strength, but also on the order in which feature events occur. We propose PhaseBreak, a white-box spectral retiming protection method that matches intermediate denoiser features to a constrained temporal rearrangement of their clean counterparts. PhaseBreak operates along the true temporal axis and uses a subject-aware mask to confine the protective perturbation to the depicted subject. Evaluations on Stable Video Diffusion and DynamiCrafter show that protected images induce greater short-term motion variation and lower temporal regularity, impeding stable motion customization from the released image.
authors: Jiashu Zhang, Xuanyou Li, Qixin Zhang
entries.title: PhaseBreak: Proactive Temporal Protection against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Animation

entries.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-aligned tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic object across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-aligned representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
entries.title: TrackTok: Semantically Persistent Tokens for Latent Video Generation

entries.abstract: We present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into 2D and 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) indoor scenes. We lift albedo, roughness, metallic and normals from diffusion-based 2D priors onto the Gaussians by back-projection, model windows and lamps as analytic area emitters, and recover their absolute radiance from ordinary LDR captures with a low-dimensional fit over unit-radiance bases. A path tracer over Gaussians and meshes then produces view-consistent shading, interreflections and soft shadows, which are composited onto the original reconstruction by differential rendering, preserving the untouched background. On synthetic, real and generated scenes, GraftRay outperforms recent insertion and inverse-rendering baselines in image fidelity and shadow accuracy at competitive cost, and users prefer its lighting and shadows over those of the baselines.
authors: Jinxin Ai, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner
entries.title: GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing

entries.abstract: Packing a 3D field into a token sequence gives every token two indices: a coordinate in the sample and a position in memory. Raster, Morton, and block-contiguous layouts change the position and leave the coordinate alone. A positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can therefore learn the memory layout rather than the object, and accuracy on the training layout cannot reveal that it has. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. It attends exactly within a coordinate-defined neighborhood, sees the whole field through pooled summaries, and rotates queries and keys with axial RoPE at token-grid coordinates. Because keys are rotated before pooling, each query-to-summary logit is a weighted sum of query-key terms evaluated at the summarized tokens' displacements from the query. The operator is equivariant to any repacking that carries coordinates, neighborhoods, summary memberships, and within-block slots along with the tokens. When evaluated on Allen WTC-11 microscopy at 262k tokens, PACK3D and a matched packed-sequence RoPE control reach comparable Dice on the training layout. Repacking the same validation volumes then costs the packed control 0.048 macro Dice on average, with a loss in all six seeds, while PACK3D changes by 0.0001. On MSD Heart and Spleen, sequence indexing again changes more predictions under repacking, at little cost in Dice. PACK3D also exceeds a parameter-matched 3D U-Net by 0.009 Dice over six seeds, and a full PACK3D layer runs within 7-31% of window-attention latency while adding a global pathway. Geometry, not storage order, should index attention over packed 3D fields. Code is available at https://github.com/amilworks/Pack3D.
authors: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
entries.title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention

entries.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
authors: Alexander Valverde, Danny Xie-Li, Zhichao Wang, Marcos V. Conde
entries.title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence

entries.abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.
authors: Xiao Cao, Fuchen Long, Yansong Qu, Wen Xiao, Xin Zhang, Xinlong Sun, Xi Chen, Zhiyong Huang
entries.title: VideoEditor-MoE: Scaling Complex Video Editing with Mixture of Experts

entries.abstract: Ultrasound videos suffer from hardware-constrained spatial resolution and signal-dependent speckle, while paired low- and high-resolution acquisitions are rarely available. We propose UltraDiff, a self-supervised framework for joint ultrasound video super-resolution and despeckling that uses a frozen pre-trained diffusion model as a plug-in prior. Rather than retraining the model, UltraDiff restores each frame by optimizing the sampler's latent seed under a range-constrained maximum a posteriori-inspired formulation. We derive a speckle-aware data-fidelity term from a Rayleigh scale-family model and characterize its relative-residual and locally variance-adaptive weighting properties. To address degeneracy near zero intensities, we introduce a stabilized surrogate fidelity that is bounded below and strictly convex in log intensity for positive observations in its unclamped form. Total-variation regularization complements the removal of mixed noise, and a temporal seed update warm-starts each frame from the optimized seed of its predecessor, accelerating the convergence. On EchoNet-LVH with simulated speckle and additive noise, UltraDiff with a natural-image prior improves peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.24\,dB over the strongest baseline, and ultrasound-related priors yield further gains. On 100 real EchoNet-Dynamic videos, UltraDiff reduces the mean absolute error of zero-shot ejection fraction prediction from 7.31 to 6.37 percentage points compared with DUP. These results support ground-truth-free ultrasound video restoration using frozen diffusion priors and a speckle-aware fidelity, without paired training data or model retraining.
authors: Chu Chen, Mingduo He, Yining Li, Yinhao Wu, Wei Tang, Yiwen Luo, Yixuan Chen, Pasquale Cascarano, Kangning Cui
entries.title: Diffusion Plug-in Priors for Self-Supervised Ultrasound Video Restoration

entries.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) localises a camera by retrieving similar geo-tagged images, and current foundation-model VPR models are accurate across cities, seasons and illumination, but not robust to adversarial perturbations: under a white-box attack on the ranking at an imperceptible budget of 1/255, SuperVLAD and BoQ keep at most 0.2% top-1 recall (R@1) on four benchmarks. We propose anchored rank-adversarial fine-tuning (ARAFT), which fine-tunes a released model with a listwise rank loss on each adversarial query's hardest positive and an anchor to the clean descriptor of the frozen pretrained model. Checkpoints are selected under a clean-accuracy budget fixed in advance, and the full trade-off is reported. Within five validation R@1 points of clean cost, plain adversarial training has no admissible checkpoint, whereas ARAFT raises robust R@1 from zero to 47.3 on SuperVLAD and 55.3 on BoQ; plain adversarial training exceeds this only at about three times the clean cost. Against unbudgeted plain adversarial training on the test sets, ARAFT matches its robust R@1 at 2/255 with about ten more clean R@1 points. At 4/255, plain adversarial training is 6-9 robust R@1 points ahead, while ARAFT still keeps its ten-point clean advantage. Developed on SuperVLAD, ARAFT transfers to BoQ without re-tuning, and its robustness holds against stronger optimisers, with no sign of gradient masking.
authors: Mostafa Kira, Bader Rasheed, Manuel Mazzara
entries.title: Anchored Rank-Adversarial Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Visual Place Recognition Models

entries.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
authors: Chenhao Zheng, Zixian Ma, Kai Li, Kanchana Ranasinghe, Jieyu Zhang, Artemis Panagopoulou, Weikai Huang, Jianxu Shangguan, Yuanyuan Tan, Silvio Savarese, Juan Carlos Niebles, Ranjay Krishna, Ran Xu, Honglu Zhou
entries.title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

entries.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.
authors: Mohamed Adjel (LAAS-GEPETTO), Kahina Chalabi (LAAS-GEPETTO), Vincent Bonnet (LAAS-GEPETTO)
entries.title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone

entries.abstract: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
authors: Ali Diba, Aisha Al-Mohannadi, Yin Yang, Muhammad Imran, Ferda Ofli
entries.title: DisasterVLG: Vision-Language Grounding and Evidence-Based Reasoning for Disaster Scene Understanding

entries.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.
authors: Zixin Su, Yangguang Lin, Zegang Peng, Yuntong Sun, Xuanyi Wang, Jiahao Wang, Qiankai Xu, Bing Yuan, Jingjia Huang, Ruyang Liu, Yanxu Hu, Yufeng Zhou, Yi Lin
entries.title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs

entries.abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.
authors: Stefan Becker, Jens Bayer, David M\"unch, Wolfgang H\"ubner
entries.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection

entries.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
authors: Yu Zhou, Xinyuan Xia, Xuankun Yang, Yinghao Yang, Wendi Chen, Bowen Liu, Jianhan Ma, Weicheng Duan, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Yanwei Li
entries.title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment

entries.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Shicheng Fang, Jiahao Lu, Yuxin Wang, Xipeng Qiu
entries.title: GTAGym: AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: 3D human motion generation plays a crucial role in game development, extended reality (XR), digital humans, and embodied simulation. Beyond motion generation, practical pipelines include rigging, retargeting, and rendering, making ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation without compromising quality valuable for real-time interactive applications. Despite promising progress, high-quality long-horizon motion generation under tight inference budgets remains challenging, owing to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget, covering text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture tasks. To enhance trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, together with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlashMotion achieves overall state-of-the-art performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation. The project page is available at https://sun-happy-ykx.github.io/FlashMotion-Project/
authors: Kaixing Yang, Xulong Tang, Ronghui Li, Xiangyue Zhang, Ziqiao Peng, Mingshuang Luo, Chenxi Zhao, Haoyu Wu, Ju Fan, Hongyan Liu, Puwei Wang, Zijiao Zeng, Jun He
entries.title: FlashMotion: Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation

entries.abstract: Video overlay removal recovers the scene beneath burned-in subtitles, karaoke lyrics, titles, credits, logos and watermarks. Generative video models now fill a known region convincingly, but in practice the region comes from a detector or a segmenter, and it is wrong in both directions: it misses strokes, halos, whole frames and whole objects, and it covers background between characters, around boxes and on genuine scene text. Erasers that treat the mask as a hole, regenerating inside and copying outside, inherit every one of these errors. We present HintErase, which treats localization as a hint, not a hole. The model sees the full, unmasked video together with a hint channel; during training the hint is corrupted the way real localizers fail, while supervision follows the true overlay. The result is a single model that removes overlay the hint missed, keeps background the hint wrongly covered, and is trained to keep genuine scene text even when the hint lands on it. For full-length releases, a streaming pipeline handles interlaced sources, shot cuts, missed and jittering hints, paste-back and audio, with memory independent of the length of the video. This report describes the approach, the pipeline that turns it into full-length deliveries, and qualitative results; video results, with input, hint and output side by side, are on the project page.
authors: Dongyang Zhang, Wei Zhang, Renjie Zou, Zhiwei Huang
entries.title: Hint, Not Hole: Localization-Robust Video Overlay Removal

entries.abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.
authors: Qiang Wen, Guotao Meng, Junhong Ruan, Hongyu Liu, Chenyang Lei, Qifeng Chen
entries.title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors

entries.abstract: Remote-sensing foundation models increasingly unify representations across sensing modalities and downstream tasks, yet their prediction mechanisms remain largely task-specific. Separate decoders, prediction heads, and objectives leave prediction fragmented across tasks. This naturally raises a question: can heterogeneous remote-sensing tasks share the prediction process? UniFlow-RS answers this question with a single latent flow-matching predictor shared across tasks. This requires addressing two key challenges: unifying heterogeneous prediction spaces and harmonizing joint optimization across tasks. First, we cast heterogeneous task outputs into structured visual targets in a common latent space, allowing them to be modeled by the same pretrained flow predictor. Task-dependent conditioning further accommodates differences in input configurations. Second, we optimize all tasks with a common Flow Matching objective, eliminating task-specific prediction losses. To mitigate optimization mismatch across tasks and modalities, we introduce Task-Modality Adaptive Timestep Sampling (TMAS), which dynamically allocates training timesteps according to the online learning state of each task-modality group. Using a single shared model, UniFlow-RS handles six tasks and thirteen datasets, surpassing recent task-specific state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while remaining competitive on the others. Beyond these benchmarks, the same checkpoint demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer across unseen datasets, task settings, occlusion conditions, and near-infrared false-color imagery, without target-specific adaptation. Codes are available at https://github.com/MindVision-AI/UniFlow-RS.
authors: Jianlong He, Liang Liao, Jing Xiao, Chaofeng Chen, Gui-Song Xia
entries.title: UniFlow-RS: Unified Generative Prediction for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Tasks

entries.abstract: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.
authors: Alexandre Garcia-Duran, Alejandro Rodriguez-Garcia, Manuel Molano-Maz\'on, Alexandre Hyafil, Srikanth Ramaswamy, Janne K. Lappalainen
entries.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion

entries.abstract: Even though many semantic segmentation methods exist that are able to perform well on many medical datasets, they are often not designed for direct use in clinical practice. The two main concerns are generalization to unseen data with a different visual appearance, e.g., images acquired using a different scanner, and efficiency in terms of computation time and required Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) memory. In this work, we employ a multi-organ segmentation model based on the SpatialConfiguration-Net (SCN), which integrates prior knowledge of the spatial configuration among the labelled organs to resolve spurious responses in the network outputs. Furthermore, we modified the architecture of the segmentation model to reduce its memory footprint as much as possible without drastically impacting the quality of the predictions. Lastly, we implemented a minimal inference script for which we optimized both execution time and required GPU memory.
authors: Franz Thaler, Christian Payer, Horst Bischof, Darko Stern
entries.title: Efficient Multi-Organ Segmentation Using SpatialConfiguration-Net with Low GPU Memory Requirements

entries.abstract:
Purpose: Healthcare AI increasingly relies on high-quality datasets, yet medical data are scarce, costly to curate, and tightly regulated in terms of data access. More critically, once medical data are leaked or accessed without authorization, data owners have limited means to prevent such data from being used to train and deploy downstream models. To address this gap, we propose DataCook, a deployment-stage usage-control framework based on anti-adversarial fingerprints.
  Materials and Methods: Specifically, DataCook transforms raw samples through a private cooking procedure that embeds anti-adversarial fingerprints. Models trained on the cooked data retain strong utility when evaluated on similarly cooked inputs, while their performance on raw inputs is reduced, making downstream model utility dependent on access to the private cooking function. We evaluate DataCook on 2D, 3D, and high-resolution medical images, as well as structured healthcare tabular data, across multiple model architectures and adaptive attack settings.
  Results: Across the evaluated settings, DataCook generally preserves authorized model utility while reducing performance on unauthorized raw inputs. The authorization-dependent behavior is observed across multiple medical imaging settings, model architectures, and adaptive attack conditions, supporting the feasibility of the proposed deployment-stage usage-control mechanism.
  Conclusion: These results demonstrate the feasibility of authorization-dependent model use at deployment, while the effectiveness of the current framework remains dependent on the specific task and evaluation metric.
authors: Sihan Shang, Jun Yan, Danli Shi, Haizhong Zheng, Shuangjia Zheng, Wei Zhao, Jiancheng Yang
entries.title: DataCook: Exploring Anti-Adversarial Fingerprints for Healthcare Data Usage Control

entries.abstract: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic cross-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FACE under few-shot cross-subject evaluation.
authors: Haiqi Liu, C. L. Philip Chen, Tong Zhang
entries.title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition

entries.abstract: Text-to-multiview (T2MV) diffusion models have shown great promise in generating multiple views of a scene from a single text prompt. While few-step backbones enable real-time T2MV generation, they often compromise key aspects of generation quality, such as per-view fidelity and cross-view consistency. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a potential solution, yet existing approaches designed for single-image diffusion do not readily extend to the few-step T2MV setting, as they neglect cross-view coordination and suffer from weak learning signals in few-step regimes. To address this, we propose MVC-ZigAL, a tailored RL finetuning framework for few-step T2MV diffusion models. Specifically, its core insights are: (1) a new MDP formulation that jointly models all generated views and assesses their collective quality via a joint-view reward; (2) a novel advantage learning strategy that exploits the performance gains of a self-refinement sampling scheme over standard sampling, yielding stronger learning signals for effective RL finetuning; and (3) a unified RL framework that extends advantage learning with a Lagrangian dual formulation for multiview-constrained optimization, balancing single-view and joint-view objectives through adaptive primal-dual updates under a self-paced threshold curriculum that harmonizes exploration and constraint enforcement. Collectively, these designs enable robust and balanced RL finetuning for few-step T2MV diffusion models, yielding substantial gains in both per-view fidelity and cross-view consistency. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyiZhang27/MVC-ZigAL.
authors: Ziyi Zhang, Li Shen, Deheng Ye, Yong Luo, Huangxuan Zhao, Meng Liu, Wei Yu, Lefei Zhang
entries.title: Refining Few-Step Text-to-Multiview Diffusion via Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: We introduce Normalized Base-2 Encoding (NB2E) as a method for encoding continuous numerical values and demonstrate that, using this input encoding, vanilla multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) successfully extrapolate four periodic waveforms without prior knowledge of their functional form. We contrast this finding with fixed Fourier encoding, which extrapolates well when the number of signal cycles over the normalized domain is an even integer and loses coherence at most other values, whereas NB2E degrades gradually away from those values and, except near odd cycle counts, remains substantially more accurate. These findings are limited to a single MLP architecture trained on one synthetic, exactly periodic, one-dimensional signal at a time, with extrapolation extending only to the end of the normalized domain. We do not propose a mechanism for this phenomenon. Rather, we present empirical observations which merit further study.
authors: Brian P. Powell, Jordan A. Caraballo-Vega, Mark L. Carroll, Thomas Maxwell, Andrew Ptak, Greg Olmschenk, Jorge Martinez-Palomera
entries.title: Extrapolation of Periodic Functions Using Binary Encoding of Continuous Numerical Values

entries.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion and flow matching models have highlighted a shift in the preferred prediction target -- moving from noise ($\varepsilon$) and velocity (v) to direct data (x) prediction -- particularly in high-dimensional settings. However, a formal explanation of why the optimal target depends on the specific properties of the data remains elusive. In this work, we provide a theoretical framework based on a generalized prediction formulation $u=kx-(1-k)n$, where $x$ represents clean data and $n$ denotes noise. This formulation accommodates arbitrary targets, of which $\varepsilon$-, v-, and x-prediction are special cases. We derive the analytical relationship between data's geometry and the optimal prediction target, offering a rigorous justification for why x-prediction becomes superior when the ambient dimension significantly exceeds the data's intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, our controlled analysis reveals how time conditioning and loss variations systematically modulate this optimal objective. While our theory identifies dimensionality as the governing factor for the optimal prediction target, the intrinsic dimension of manifold-bound data is typically intractable to estimate in practice. To bridge this gap, we propose k-Diff, a framework that employs a data-driven approach to learn the optimal prediction parameter k directly from data, bypassing the need for explicit dimension estimation. Extensive experiments in both latent-space and pixel-space image generation demonstrate that k-Diff consistently outperforms fixed-target baselines across varying architectures and data scales, providing a principled and automated approach to enhancing generative performance.
authors: Qing Jin, Chaoyang Wang
entries.title: Understanding and Learning Prediction Targets in Diffusion Models

entries.abstract: Incorporating diffusion-generated synthetic data into adversarial training (AT) has been shown to substantially improve the training of robust image classifiers. In this work, we extend the role of diffusion models beyond merely generating synthetic data, examining whether their internal representations, which encode meaningful features of the data, can provide additional benefits for robust classifier training. Through systematic experiments, we show that diffusion models offer representations that are both diverse and partially robust, and that explicitly incorporating diffusion representations as an auxiliary learning signal during AT consistently improves robustness across settings. Furthermore, our representation analysis indicates that incorporating diffusion models into AT encourages more disentangled features, while diffusion representations and diffusion-generated synthetic data play complementary roles in shaping representations. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet validate these findings, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly leveraging diffusion representations and synthetic data within AT.
authors: Pin-Han Huang, Shang-Tse Chen, Hsuan-Tien Lin
entries.title: Expanding the Role of Diffusion Models for Robust Classifier Training

entries.abstract: Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and distributional alignment of within-plan public-space advantage (PIAD). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback reduces IPD and PIAD across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.
authors: Zhuoyang Jiang, Dongqing Zhang, Qingxiang Liu, Yuxuan Liang
entries.title: Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement

entries.abstract: Oscillations and synchronization are widely believed to play a fundamental role in representation and computation. However, existing machine learning approaches based on synchronization dynamics have largely been confined to specialized settings such as object discovery, with limited evidence of scalability to standard vision benchmarks or logic reasoning tasks. We propose the Winfree Oscillatory Neural Network (WONN), a dynamical neural architecture based on generalized Winfree dynamics. WONN evolves representations on the torus $(S^1)^d$ through structured oscillatory interactions, combining phase-based inductive biases with flexible and hierarchical interaction mechanisms instantiated as either fixed trigonometric mappings or learnable neural networks. We evaluate WONN on image recognition and complex reasoning tasks, including CIFAR, ImageNet, Maze-hard, and Sudoku. Across these domains, WONN achieves competitive or superior performance with strong parameter efficiency. In particular, WONN is, to our knowledge, the first synchronization-based oscillatory architecture to scale competitively to ImageNet-1K. Furthermore, on Maze-hard, WONN achieves 80.1% accuracy using only 1% of the parameters of prior state-of-the-art models. These results suggest that structured oscillatory dynamics provide a scalable and parameter-efficient alternative to conventional neural architectures.
authors: Jiawen Dai, Yue Song
entries.title: Winfree Oscillatory Neural Network

entries.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely used, but understanding what they actually learn remains difficult. A major obstacle is that individual neurons often respond to multiple unrelated concepts, obscuring the network's internal decision process. Existing approaches, such as sparse autoencoders, can disentangle these mixed signals into more meaningful, ``monosemantic'' features, but typically introduce approximation errors that may degrade downstream performance. Consequently, these methods exhibit a Pareto frontier between monosemanticity and functional faithfulness. To address this, we introduce DUNE (disentangling units with no error), a method that decomposes DNN neurons into more monosemantic subunits while preserving their original function by design. DUNE identifies concept-specific contributions from the preceding layer and re-routes them into separate subunits whose aggregation exactly recovers the original activation. DUNE can be applied directly to pretrained models, without labels or training of an auxiliary model. Across several models, including DINOv2, DUNE achieves state-of-the-art or competitive monosemanticity while exactly preserving functional faithfulness, substantially advancing the existing Pareto frontier between these properties. DUNE operates efficiently and enables fine-grained interventions such as concept-specific steering.
authors: Do\u{g}ukan Ba\u{g}c{\i}, Bernt Schiele, Simone Schaub-Meyer, Jonas Fischer, Robin Hesse
entries.title: DUNE: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons Without Losing Predictive Performance

entries.abstract: Background: Deep learning can classify thyroid nodules on ultrasound, but discrimination alone does not establish clinical reliability. We developed a calibrated deep-ensemble framework with uncertainty-aware selective prediction and conservative image-based triage. Methods: Nested five-fold cross-validation with three-fold inner architecture selection chose ConvNeXt-Tiny with a squeeze-and-excitation block, used to build a deterministic five-member ensemble. Training, early-stopping, calibration, and threshold subsets were separated within each fold; outer-test data remained isolated. Mutual information (MI), predictive variance, and maximum-softmax-probability (MSP) uncertainty were compared by risk-coverage and triage analyses, and predictive values across assumed malignancy prevalences of 5%-70%. The frozen TN5000 ensemble was applied to TN3K without recalibration. Results: On TN5000, pooled out-of-fold AUC-ROC was 0.9377, average precision 0.9708, expected calibration error 0.0138, and Brier score 0.0827. Under the primary MI-guided policy, 8.86% of images received a No-FNA suggestion, 60.00% an FNA recommendation, and 31.14% radiologist review; of 3574 malignant images, 14 (0.39%) received No-FNA and 708 (19.81%) review. Predictive variance and MSP ranked errors better than MI (AURC, AUGRC); no measure optimized all triage outcomes. Across prevalences of 5%-70%, NPV ranged 99.95%-97.93% and PPV 29.28%-94.75%. On TN3K, AUC-ROC was 0.7870, average precision 0.7254, expected calibration error 0.1899, and radiologist-review rate 83.7%. Conclusion: The ensemble showed strong internal discrimination and calibration, but performance deteriorated substantially on TN3K, indicating limited transportability under dataset shift. Multicentre validation, site-specific recalibration, threshold validation, and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical use.
authors: Md. Sadibul Hasan Sadib, Md. Mohayminul Mukit, Rahmatul Kabir Rasel Sarker, Tahmid Alam Tamim, Md. Nazmul Hasan, Md. Monir Hossain Shimul
entries.title: Calibrated selective prediction using deep ensembles for thyroid nodule ultrasound classification under dataset shift

entries.abstract: Pixel-level supervision in medical image segmentation ignores the geometric priors of the target region. Chan-Vese losses restore region-level priors and boundary regularity but do not characterise local boundary geometry. We propose the Deep Active Contour and Mean Curvature (DACMC) loss, which embeds the mean curvature of the predicted boundary in the Chan-Vese region functional; a fixed fourth-order-accurate convolution kernel evaluates curvature without explicit differentiation. The loss adds no trainable parameters and no inference cost, increases training time by 4.8%, and uses one hyper-parameter lambda = 10^-3 shared by all settings. We evaluate DACMC on liver CT, spleen MRI and ISIC dermoscopy images with U-Net and CE-Net backbones, four metrics (DSC, HD95, JS, ASD) and four competing losses under an identical protocol, together with a five-point lambda sweep, a wall-clock cost measurement and a five-seed replication with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. DACMC ranks first or second in Dice in five of the six dataset-backbone settings, most consistently in distance metrics. On spleen MRI it reduces HD95 and ASD to 16.28 and 1.90 mm, and on ISIC dermoscopy it reduces HD95 to 7.08 mm. Dice varies by 0.0023 across five lambda values spanning three orders of magnitude; degradation appears only when curvature dominates. Five-seed replication shows that curvature stabilises training and removes occasional severe failures, although mean differences from the closest competing loss do not reach statistical significance at five seeds. DACMC imposes second-order geometric regularity on segmentation boundaries at low overhead, with the clearest benefit for small or scale-varying targets. Limitations include dataset size and partitioning, classical backbones and losses, and restriction to 2-D single-organ images.
authors: Xiao-qiang Zhai, Zhi-feng Pang, Peng Zheng, Ze-wen Li, Yan-zhe Hou
entries.title: Medical Image Segmentation based on Deep Active Contour and Mean Curvature Loss Function

entries.abstract: 3D simulation platforms are critical for autonomous driving because they enable end-to-end policy evaluation, thereby reducing development costs and improving safety. In recent years, neural simulation has become predominant, with methods such as NuRec playing a central role; however, these methods remain relatively slow and typically require per-scene tuning.
