(1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.
authors: Zengqing Wu, Chuan Xiao
entries.title: When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models

entries.abstract: With the rapid development of LLMs, increasing attention has been paid to whether they can reliably generate complete and legally valid judicial documents. This calls for a benchmark capable of evaluating whether models can accurately apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues, including claims, charges, penalties, and monetary obligations. However, existing benchmarks typically focus on isolated legal tasks or coarse-grained evaluation. We introduce ChJGBench, a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal, and administrative cases. Built from 3,462 real-world judgments, ChJGBench provides a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework comprising 13 metric types and adopts a hybrid paradigm. Experiments reveal no uniform advantage for legal-domain models over general-purpose models, with model strengths varying across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases continue to present substantial challenges.
authors: Yinghao Hu, Linggang Kong, Qian Xiao, Yuting Huang, Yunlong Zhang, Yujie Zhang, Yiquan Wu, Fei Duan, Kaisong Song, Jun Lin, Kun Kuang, Fei Wu
entries.title: ChJGBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Legal Judgment Generation with Diagnostic Evaluation

entries.abstract: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Giannis Nikolentzos, Polykarpos Meladianos, Michalis Vazirgiannis
entries.title: Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights

entries.abstract: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/A412/.
authors: Tingna Xie, Ming Wang, Shi Feng, Yongkang Liu
entries.title: Can Agents Relive Past Experiences? Diagnosing Event-Affect Decoupling in Affective-Episodic Retrospection

entries.abstract:
Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked.
  We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.
authors: Ragini Menon, Sabine Tittel
entries.title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard

entries.abstract: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.
authors: Kazi Rafat, Afifa Imran, Md. Ismail Hossain, Md. Romzan Ali, Fuad Rahman, Sifat Momen, Shafin Rahman, Nabeel Mohammed
entries.title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation

entries.abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Purusharth Malik, Pasunuti Prasanjith, Daksh Maan, Parijat Chatterjee, Avinash Benki
entries.title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training

entries.abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, Lorenzo Cavallaro
entries.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs

entries.abstract: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.
authors: Lichen Li, Ziping Dong, Sicheng Feng, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
entries.title: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models

entries.abstract: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.
authors: Shane Steinert-Threlkeld, Jakub Szymanik
entries.title: Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals

entries.abstract: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. We present HeriKGQA, a knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, leaving computation to SPARQL and deterministic code. Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology aligning W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results and temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer, with error correction guarding each LLM step. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.
authors: Lingxiao Kong, Vasileios Arampatzakis, Vasileios Sevetlidis, George Pavlidis, Zeyd Boukhers
entries.title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data

entries.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.
authors: Sujan Maharjan, Lu Liu
entries.title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models

entries.abstract: Even though various speech data sets are available in Hungarian, there is a lack of a general overview about their types and sizes. To fill in this gap, we provide a survey of available data sets in spoken Hungarian in five categories (e.g., monolingual, Hungarian part of multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections). In total, the estimated size of available data is about 2800 hours (across 7500 speakers) and it represents a rich spoken language diversity. However, the distribution of the data and its alignment to real-life (e.g. speech recognition) tasks is far from optimal indicating the need for additional larger-scale natural language speech data sets. Our survey presents an overview of available data sets for Hungarian explaining their strengths and weaknesses which is useful for researchers working on Hungarian across disciplines. In addition, our survey serves as a starting point towards a unified foundational speech model specific to Hungarian.
authors: P\'eter Mihajlik, Katalin M\'ady, Anna Koh\'ari, Fruzsina S\'ara Vargha, G\'abor Kiss, Tekla Etelka Gr\'aczi, A. Seza Do\u{g}ru\"oz
entries.title: Is Spoken Hungarian Low-resource?: A Quantitative Survey of Hungarian Speech Data Sets

entries.abstract: Punctuation marks often mark phrase boundaries, carrying linguistic information. Therefore, punctuation marks' abundance and feasibility as proxies of linguistic structure has led to suggestions that using punctuation marks to optimise on phrasal structure may help language models (LMs) improve their representations of argument, semantic, and syntactic structures. In this paper, we test the above claim in English across three primary LM architectures: decoder-only, encoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs, by complementing traditional token prediction with punctuation restoration (PR). Our evidence, collected at the <1B parameter scale, suggests that optimising for boundary prediction does not necessarily guarantee higher-quality structural representation in decoder-only, encoder-decoder, and encoder-only LMs, failing to improve performance on downstream tasks that require understanding structure in linguistic input.
authors: Michael Zhou, Markus Frohmann, Junghyun Min, En-Shiun Annie Lee
entries.title: Better Boundary Prediction Does Not Guarantee Better Structural Representation

entries.abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.
authors: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
entries.title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs

entries.abstract: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.
authors: Jeffrey M. Girard, Antony D'Avirro, Jason Z. Zheng, Jacqueline R. Vertino, Benjamin Peloquin
entries.title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls

entries.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.
authors: Haoyi Qiu, Akshat Agarwal
entries.title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models

entries.abstract: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.
authors: Jessica Lundin, Katherine Rosenfeld, David Adelani, Geoffrey Mosoti Nyakiongora, Halfan Ngowo, Sloan Coffin, Ralph Abboud, Guillaume Chabot-Couture
entries.title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning

entries.abstract: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, ignoring behavioral patterns that emerge across sequences of messages from the same sender. We study outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, where the goal is to predict at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam. Using a proprietary production database of 43,741 outbound SMS messages with UTC transmission timestamps and carrier delivery statuses, we report three sets of results. On an 8,749-message held-out test set, a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. A deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382, and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate, class-balanced 20,000-message production evaluation set; these results are not directly comparable with the held-out test results. We also describe TemporalBertSpam, an architecture that encodes each sender's message history with a causal Transformer, and outline the same-split evaluation needed to measure its contribution.
authors: Fariz Zeynalov, Razim Mammadli
entries.title: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models

entries.abstract: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.
authors: Hongyu Li, Zhan Yu, Zhe Zhao, Kimmo Yan, Xiong Kuang, Renfen Hu
entries.title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features

entries.abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
authors: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, Zhuoshi Tong, Haisen Liao, Sicheng Zhou
entries.title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue

entries.abstract: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Daksh Maan, Avinash Benki, Parijat Chatterjee, Pasunuti Prasanjith, Purusharth Malik
entries.title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.
authors: Husein Zolkepli
entries.title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text

entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.
authors: Chao Chen, Shanshan Lin, Dongsheng Hong, Sibo Ju, Wenjie Yang, Sihong Xie, Xiangwen Liao
entries.title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning

entries.abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.
authors: Xin Zhang, Victor S. Sheng
entries.title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference

entries.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
authors: Minh-Anh Nguyen
entries.title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation

entries.abstract: Millions of Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) users lack reliable automatic translation tools. Existing systems are limited by data scarcity, unidirectional design, and computationally expensive architectures that are not suitable for low-resource deployment. We introduce IsharaBART, a bidirectional generative framework for gloss-sentence translation in BdSL. IsharaBART uses Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART)-based conditional language modeling with denoising learning objectives. We developed a parallel dataset of 1,000 professionally annotated gloss-sentence pairs, balanced across tenses and structures. We expanded the dataset to 4,831 pairs through four augmentation techniques: rule-based tense transformations, masked token substitutions, back-translation, and one-shot prompting. A compact denoising sequence-to-sequence model was pre-trained from scratch on monolingual Bangla text from six different corpora, then fine-tuned on the annotated and augmented datasets. We compare IsharaBART against four larger baseline models under identical conditions, where it achieves comparable or superior bidirectional performance. On the gloss-to-sentence (G2S) task, it attains Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU-4) score up to 51.7, and on the sentence-to-gloss (S2G) task, it achieves 61.40, outperforming multilingual models despite having fewer than 10% of the parameters. Ablation studies demonstrate that pre-training provides 62.5-90.4% faster convergence and 11.5-118% higher BLEU-4 than scratch. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces trainable parameters by 99.3%, but with 28.0-52.2% loss of BLEU-4 compared to full-parameter fine-tuning.
authors: Aonmoy Das, Ananna Dev Aishi, Md. Fazlul Kader
entries.title: IsharaBART: An efficient BART-Based Framework for Low-Resource Bangla Sign Language Translation

entries.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
authors: Sikui Zhang, Haowei Liu, Ziyun Gan, Chunfeng Yuan, Guangze Gao, Nian Liu, Boyu Cai, Bo Li, Xiaolei Lv, Jun Gao, Bing Li, Weiming Hu
entries.title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression

entries.abstract: EmbeddingGemma-300M is a small open embedder, and used as released it finds the right passage first for 60.8% of the Kazakh Belebele retrieval questions. We present Saidzoda-Kazakh-EmbeddingGemma-300M, the same model fully fine-tuned for one epoch on 208,511 pairs: 166,263 Kazakh questions that our own language model wrote about source passages from encyclopedias, Wikipedia, news and books, each checked by a second model, plus English and Russian replay. On Kazakh Belebele, recall@1 rises from 60.8% to 78.0% and recall@10 from 76.3% to 91.4%. Our model scores above 161 of the 194 models with a published MTEB score on the same test, among them OpenAI text-embedding-3-large (47.1%). The other 33 score higher: the ten best are large multi-billion-parameter or closed models, reaching up to 92.2%, and at least 9 are open models of up to 0.6B parameters, the smallest with 339M. We also scored 6 Kazakh-specific embedders shared on Hugging Face with the same code in one run: our model (77.3% there) is ahead of 4 of them, including the two E5-base models of similar size (72.6% and 69.0%), and behind kaz-embedder (86.0%, three towers with 1,695M parameters in total) and a BGE-M3 fine-tune (81.0%); at recall@10 its interval overlaps those of its nearest neighbours on both sides. Our four-language model, trained with a capped share of the same Kazakh pairs, is 2.8 points lower at recall@1, with overlapping recall@10 intervals. The Kazakh model also scores higher than the released model on the Uzbek and Kyrgyz versions of Belebele, but our Tajik model, trained without any Turkic pairs, gains as much there, so these gains are not specific to Kazakh training. Our Kazakh Wikipedia test questions come from the same generator family as the training questions, so we rest the main claims on Belebele.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Faroiz Bobokhon, Aibek Shokanuly
entries.title: Saidzoda-Kazakh-EmbeddingGemma-300M: How Far One Epoch of Generated Questions Takes a Small Kazakh Embedder

entries.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.
authors: Wenhong Zhu, Xuefeng Li, Jiashuo Zhang, Yu Chen, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu
entries.title: daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving

entries.abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question about a text in one pass: the question, the options (each with a name and a description) and the text form one sequence of at most 512 tokens, the window, in the English release. A longer text is silently cut at the end, and we measure what that costs. Test documents place a held-out row's text, the evidence, at a chosen token offset among distractor text; 177 items, five tasks, three checkpoints (released, short-row fine-tune, long-document fine-tune), four window sizes and 93,275 scored requests. When the evidence lies beyond the window, accuracy falls to 26.4% for the released checkpoint (27.2% for both fine-tunes), near the 27.0% of guessing and below the 35.6% of always giving the commonest label. Confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.50 to 0.55 for telling cut from read requests; 0.5 = chance), and the runtime's truncation flag also fires on requests whose evidence was visible. The released checkpoint reads visible evidence badly once text precedes it: 38.5% pooled against 60% when the evidence comes first, so a larger window alone gains +6.2 points. Fine-tuning on long documents adds +27.6 points on visible evidence over the short-row fine-tune (95% interval +22.3 to +33.1) and nothing on cut evidence. That is an in-family result: training rows and test documents share generator and question types, and the main filler is of the training kind. With encyclopedic filler never seen in training the gain is +13.2 (+9.9 to +16.6), with rows of other tasks as filler -2.0. Among training-free rearrangements a 312-token window scan helps most (+11.9 points over the default for the released checkpoint) at six to eleven forward passes. Documents are synthetic, labels are LLM-made and one backbone is studied, so these diagnose this model, not long documents in general.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Allan Kevin T
entries.title: Where in the Input Does a One-Pass Decision Encoder Look?

entries.abstract: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.
authors: Daniil Makovetskii, Ivan Bondarenko
entries.title: EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning

entries.abstract: This paper describes the approach of the Unibuc - NLP team in tackling the "Voight-Kampff" Generative AI Detection task from PAN at CLEF 2025. In the Subtask 1: Voight-Kampff AI Detection Sensitivity we have explored different approaches of leveraging embeddings extracted from LLMs, using either classical ML models or further fine-tuning LLMs with a classification head for the downstream binary classification task. Our experiments showed that using a majority vote ensemble of classical ML models (Light GBM, XGB, Logistic Regression and SVM) is comparable with fine-tuning for downstream task achieving around 99.4% F1 score. For the Subtask 2: Human-AI Collaborative Text Classification we explored a way of combining features at different layers extracted using transformer backbone with layer-wise projection and attentive pooling which proved modest results.
authors: Teodor Marchitan, Claudiu Creanga, Liviu P. Dinu
entries.title: Unibuc - NLP at "Voight-Kampff" Generative AI Detection PAN 2025

entries.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.
authors: Chunkit Chan, Kawai Chung, Sze Heng Douglas Kwok, Yuxuan Liu, Yauwai Yim, Tianshi Zheng, Haochen Shi, Qing Zong, Wong Kai Chung, Pak Hin Lau, Calvin Yang, Yifan Gao, Xiaoman Pan, Ginny Wong, Simon See, Yangqiu Song
entries.title: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses

entries.abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) companies develop and deliver a one-of-a-kind product in response to a client's orders. To prepare resources for development beforehand, companies estimate dates when they will receive orders from clients in their sales process, called scheduled order dates. However, dates when the companies actually receive orders can differ from the scheduled order dates. This difference increases costs in the development. If the difference could be forecasted before receiving orders, companies could optimize their resource preparation. Towards reducing the costs, we introduce sales delay forecasting, a novel task of forecasting delay days from the scheduled order dates during sales process where sales representatives (sales reps) interact with the clients to receive orders. Sales delay forecasting is challenging because the sales process progress inherently involves uncertainty and depends on the client's willingness to order. To address this task, we propose confidence features which represent sales reps' confidence as a proxy measure of the client's willingness to order. To represent it, our method extracts dates of future sales events anticipated by sales reps from textual reports. To consider whether the confidence objectively looks reasonable, we also introduce status features which describe sales process status based on current date and past events. In experiments using real sales data, our method achieved a 16% lower mean absolute error compared with a feature-based baseline similar to a prior work. Moreover, our method outperformed non-feature-based baselines using large language models, indicating that it is crucial to explicitly create our features.
authors: Masaya Tsunokake, Yuta Koreeda, Yuhei Niwa, Terufumi Morishita, Teppei Inoue, Hiroaki Ozaki, Yasuhiro Sogawa
entries.title: Forecasting Sales Delay through Time-aware Analysis of Sales Events in Textual Reports

entries.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.
authors: Antal van den Bosch
entries.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding

entries.abstract: To keep long interaction contexts tractable, stepwise group-relative training for multi-turn LLM agents materializes each source trajectory into multiple response rows and valid tokens. This expansion creates an outer-accounting problem distinct from within-trajectory credit assignment: row-based outcome statistics can count one episode outcome multiple times, while token-level reduction can assign unequal aggregate objective mass across trajectories. We term these effects outcome-statistics multiplicity and objective-mass imbalance. We introduce Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA), a two-component method that makes both accounting choices explicit. Outcome Alignment computes outcome statistics over unique source trajectories, while Mass Alignment controls aggregate objective mass after within-trajectory aggregation of optimizer-native token objectives. Neither redesigns the base optimizer's credit assignment, importance ratios, or clipping. Across matched ALFWorld GRPO comparisons at two model scales, where failed trajectories typically expand much more than successful ones, OMA improves matched-horizon endpoint success by 7.0-9.4 percentage points. Ordinary WebShop exhibits weak or reversed expansion-outcome coupling and correspondingly mixed effects, whereas in a success-oriented WebShop setting, WebShop-SOL, OMA improves success nAUC from 0.399 to 0.511. Component ablations and GiGPO and GSPO comparisons further support component separability and cross-optimizer compatibility. These results show that trajectory expansion always defines an implicit weighting rule, but its practical effect depends on how expansion couples to outcomes and optimizer-native updates.
authors: Dawei Zhang, Yubin Huangfu, Jessica Fan, Boyu Wei, Likang Wu, Hongke Zhao, Ming He, Zhu Teng
entries.title: Outcome-Mass Alignment: Controlling Length-Dependent Trajectory Influence in Multi-Turn LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.
authors: Aarne Talman, Stergios Chatzikyriakidis
entries.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models

entries.abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
authors: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger
entries.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models

entries.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.
authors: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter
entries.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training

entries.abstract: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.
authors: Harras Mansoor, Muhammad Wisal, Hassan Bhatti, Masood Shakir
entries.title: Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR

entries.abstract: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.
authors: Alex Jiang, Didier Schwab, Chuyuan Li
entries.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection

entries.abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

entries.abstract:
Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests.
  Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT
authors: Mohamed Zakaria Kurdi
entries.title: Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech

entries.abstract: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.
authors: Daniel Denley, Robert L. Nicol, Mike J. Chantler
entries.title: Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models

entries.abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.
authors: \'I\~nigo Zubeldia, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Miles Cranmer
entries.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers

entries.abstract: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
entries.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks

entries.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
authors: Xinheng Ding, Seyyed Saeid Cheshmi, Ziyang Zhang, Tairan Chen, Wenya Xie, Yu Hou, Rui Zhang, Zirui Liu
entries.title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution

entries.abstract: Provably secure linguistic steganography assumes that the receiver recovers the sender's tokens, but a text channel delivers only text, and ambiguous tokenizations break extraction. Existing fixes change the distribution, synchronize whole pools of tokens at a capacity that collapses with large vocabularies, or track several token histories. We prove that if extraction is exact and error-free across full-support language models, a single-history receiver is confined to a prefix-free candidate set at every step -- even if it reads the entire future text and the sender constrains later steps -- and must therefore give up the stop entropy, the entropy of deciding whether each prefix token ends there. Fixing these stop decisions on the prefix forest with shared randomness yields coin projection: a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, preserves ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key. Across English, Chinese and Japanese, ambiguous text is rare (at most 11 in 1,000 tokens), yet the stop entropy at word and morpheme prefixes takes 7.2-9.0% of the entropy at every step; SyncPool's further loss comes from space and single-byte UTF-8 hubs that merge subtrees while carrying almost no stop uncertainty. Coin projection keeps 91-93% of the string entropy for the coder at every vocabulary size; with the full vocabulary, it turns 2.16-6.85 times as much entropy into message bits as SyncPool and recovers every completed message.
authors: Feng Jiang
entries.title: Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography

entries.abstract: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.
authors: Paul Grunenwald, Beno\^it Crabb\'e, Guillaume Wisniewski, Pirmin Lemberger
entries.title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification

entries.abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.
authors: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
entries.title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models
